newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Orange branches out into tree masts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Orange branches out into tree masts.

text.p: COCKERMOUTH, England, - Orange Plc, a British mobile telephone company, on Monday unveiled the first telecommunications mast in Europe disguised to look like a tree -- at least from a distance.

In an attempt to quell mounting criticism by conservationists, incensed at a growing army of telecom masts springing up across Britain, Orange has created what it calls "loquentes per arbores" -- talking through trees.

Standing 12 metres (40 feet) high on the edge of the picturesque Lake District region, the experimental steel and plastic creation is supposed to look like a conifer and blend in with the real trees in the area.
In driving rain and gale-force winds the American- designed tree "which towers over organic trees in the area" looked a little forlorn, standing isolated in its own enclosure in a muddy field.
But in an attempt to woo wildlife, Orange has attached a nesting box for birds onto one of the steel tubes which are coated to make them look like bark.
The actual aerials are in the plastic branches at the top of the tow, hidden by false foliage.
The company said it would take six months to finish testing whether the design would stand up to nature -- and conservationist scrutiny.

Orange said it was the first mobile phone company in Britain to test the new "green" design and although the group claimed it had won the approval of local residents, it remains to be seen whether it will catch on.
Brushing off criticism that the tree looked at best American, the company said that the design of any such future transmitters would be refined to fit better into the British environment.
"We are branching out into a new area, this is symbolic of the fact that the Orange network is growing", Colin Tucker, group technical and operations director told a news conference.

Many residents of rural areas targeted by mobile phone companies like Orange and its rivals Vodafone, Cable and Wireless's Mercury unit and British Telecommunciations' Cellnet Business, are outraged by the proliferation of telecoms towers.
While mobile phone companies try to plug the gaps in their national network and improve reception, around 8,000 masts already straddle the country, catering for around six million mobile phone users.
Orange, partly owned by Hongkong conglomerate Hutchison Whampoa, and British Aerospace, now covers 92 percent of the British population and plans to cover 96 percent by the end of this year.
This year, the company plans to invest more than 250 million pounds ($405 million) in its network and by the end of the year it will have 3,300 sites.
Mobile phone groups, whose market has grown meteorically over the last decade, are required to cover 90 percent of the country by the year 2000 under terms of their license.
According to planning law operators can install, alter, or replace masts up to 15 metres high without needing to submit a planning application -- unless they are in certain protected areas.
